title: In his image (Genesis 1:26–31)
hookLine: humans made in God's image, male and female, and it was very good

lines: A KING'S STATUE IN A FAR-OFF TOWN.
cards: A carved stone king stands in a town square, weeks from his palace. Everyone who passes gets the message: this land is his, his authority reaches here. The image stands in for the king.
Some scholars think the first hearers of today's verse would have known statues like that. Hold that picture. On the sixth day, after the land animals, the story slows down.
God doesn't just say let there be. God says let us make. And what gets made is a creature that carries an image.

teach.h: TSELEM: AN IMAGE, A CARVED FIGURE.
teach.b: Here's verse twenty-seven in the King James Bible: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
The Hebrew word for image is tselem, used elsewhere in the Bible for a carved figure. In Latin, imago Dei, the image of God.
Notice who's included: male and female, together, from the first line about people. Not a king, not a priest, not one special family. Every human.
If those scholars are right, that's the twist: in Genesis, it isn't a ruler who carries God's image into the world. It's everyone.

teach.h: WHAT IS THE IMAGE? WHO IS US?
teach.b: What the image actually is, the text doesn't spell out. Christians have suggested reason, or love, or the ability to make things, or the job in the next verse: to fill the earth and care for it as God's stand-ins.
Some hold several at once. Another puzzle: let us make. Who is us?
Some Christians, from early church writers on, hear a hint of the Trinity. Some Jewish commentators hear God speaking with the heavenly court. Others hear a plural of majesty, like a royal we.
Then the chapter ends with God looking at everything one last time: "and, behold, it was very good." Not just good, like the other days. Very good.

teach.h: IN THE IMAGE OF GOD CREATED HE HIM.
teach.b: Christian traditions differ on what happened to the image after the garden. But Christians have used this verse to argue that no person can be owned, erased, or treated as nobody.

how: Christian teaching on human dignity often starts from the image of God, and church statements cite Genesis 1:27 when speaking about the worth of every person, from the unborn to the dying, the poor and the stranger.

games.q: you're an ancient king, and you can't be everywhere in your empire. how do you show your rule reaches a far-off town?
o: you set up a statue of yourself in the square.
games.why: kings set up images of themselves. in Genesis, it isn't a ruler who carries God's image into the world. it's every human being.

practice: Bring a face to mind: someone you love, someone you pass every day and barely see, or someone you find hard.
Picture it clearly, and hold the old idea next to it: this face carries an image, like a statue in the town square, not because of anything this person has done, just because they're human.
If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
